findings.claim: 'Describe two features' (4 marks) ... 'Explain why' (8 marks) ... 'Make and defend a judgement' (16 marks) ... The 12-mark historic environment essay
findings.truth: 'Explain why' is 12 marks; the 16-mark stem is 'How far do you agree?'; 'Describe two features' is set only on the historic environment; there is no 12-mark historic environment essay. That section is 16 marks in total (4 + 8 + 4).
findings.evidence: spec assessment section: Paper 1, 1h20, 52 marks - 16 historic environment, 36 thematic study, up to 4 SPaG on Q5/6

findings.claim: Three of six questions use 'Describe two features' on thematic-study content; two 'Explain why' questions are set at 8 marks
findings.truth: 'Describe two features' is set only on the historic environment. The thematic study sets a 4-mark similarity/difference question, a 12-mark 'Explain why' and a 16-mark 'How far do you agree'. Questions rebuilt to those forms with new mark schemes.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section

findings.claim: Miranda Kaufmann has documented over sixty parish baptisms of Africans in Tudor England between 1500 and 1640
findings.truth: Kaufmann's published research identifies more than 360 Africans in England between 1500 and 1640 - the figure this unit already uses in lesson 5. The 'sixty parish baptisms' number cannot be traced.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with L5 of this unit; Miranda Kaufmann, Africans in Britain 1500-1640 database

findings.claim: Examiners reward answers that move between periods ... is explicitly capped by examiners ... Examiners reward judgements anchored to specific dates
findings.truth: Invented examiner behaviour; no board publishes these rules. Reworded as advice about strong answers.
findings.evidence: house rule: no invented exam claims

findings.claim: Comma-list answers ('Institutions, religion, economic influences, and attitudes in society') and bare-date answers ('1948.', '1905.', '1290.')
findings.truth: List answers fail the validator and bare dates teach nothing. Rewritten as one idea each with a few words of substance.
findings.evidence: checker brief, flashcard rules

findings.claim: a boundary running roughly along the Roman road of Watling Street, from London to Chester
findings.truth: Watling Street ran from Dover through London and St Albans to Wroxeter in Shropshire. It did not run to Chester.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Watling Street'

findings.claim: In 878 ... Alfred the Great agreed the Treaty of Wedmore. Guthrum ... accepted a boundary
findings.truth: The 878 agreement at Wedmore was the peace and Guthrum's baptism. The Watling Street boundary survives in a separate written text, the Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum, which historians usually date to the 880s. One clause added; the familiar 878 shorthand kept.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Watling Street' (Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum names the road as the boundary)

findings.claim: Three 'Describe two features' questions on thematic content and two 'Explain why' questions set at 8 marks
findings.truth: Rebuilt to the thematic forms: 4-mark similarity/difference, 12-mark 'Explain why', 16-mark 'How far do you agree'.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section

findings.claim: the Heathen Army
findings.truth: The force is normally called the Great Heathen Army (or Great Army). The short form is understandable but is not the name students will meet in sources or textbooks.
findings.evidence: standard naming in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle tradition

findings.claim: Bare answers ('865.', '878.', 'Around 1,500.') and list answers ('Sky and law (also egg, knife, they, them, their).')
findings.truth: Rewritten as one idea each with supporting substance.
findings.evidence: checker brief, flashcard rules

findings.claim: Jorvik issued silver pennies stamped with the names of its kings, including Cnut and the Anglo-Scandinavian moneyer Hildulf
findings.truth: The 'Cnut' on the York coinage is a Viking king of York of about 900, not the Cnut of 1016 that the previous lesson introduces, so the sentence invites a serious confusion. The moneyer's name cannot be verified. Both specifics removed.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with L2 of this unit; no traceable source for the moneyer

findings.claim: Three 'Describe two features' questions on thematic content, one 'Explain the importance' question, and 'Explain why' set at 8 marks; a mark scheme claiming 'The kingdom's existence required the Treaty of Wedmore framework'
findings.truth: 'Explain the importance' is not set on this paper. Rebuilt to the thematic forms. The causal claim is also wrong: the Viking kingdom of York began in 866, twelve years before the 878 agreement, and York lay outside its terms.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section; lesson 3 dates York's capture to 866

findings.claim: Bare answers ('Jorvik.', 'Eoforwic.', '866.') and list answers
findings.truth: Rewritten as one idea each with supporting substance.
findings.evidence: checker brief, flashcard rules

findings.claim: Hanseatic merchants ran a fortified trading enclave ... granted special privileges by Henry III in 1281
findings.truth: Henry III died in 1272, so he cannot have granted anything in 1281. The London Hanse is first recorded as one organisation in 1282, and Edward I confirmed its trading privileges in the Carta Mercatoria of 1303. Elizabeth I closed the Steelyard in 1598.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Steelyard'

findings.claim: Hundreds of Jewish people died after taking refuge there [Clifford's Tower, 1190]
findings.truth: About 150 Jewish people died at Clifford's Tower on 16 March 1190, most of them by their own hand rather than surrender to the mob.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, "Clifford's Tower"

findings.claim: Three 'Describe two features' questions on thematic content and two 'Explain why' questions set at 8 marks
findings.truth: Rebuilt to the thematic forms: 4-mark similarity/difference, 12-mark 'Explain why', 16-mark 'How far do you agree'.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section

findings.claim: By 1450, around 1.5% of England's population was made up of recorded aliens
findings.truth: The 1440 alien subsidy recorded roughly 16,000 aliens in a population of about two million, which is closer to 1%. The 1.5% figure could not be verified, so it is left but flagged.
findings.evidence: England's Immigrants 1330-1550 project figures

findings.claim: Bare answers ('1348-49.') and the Steelyard card naming Henry III in 1281
findings.truth: Rewritten with substance and with the corrected grant.
findings.evidence: checker brief; Wikipedia, 'Steelyard'

findings.claim: In 1685, Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes ... Charles II encouraged the arrivals through royal proclamations promising denization
findings.truth: Charles II died in February 1685, eight months before the revocation in October 1685. His denization proclamation for French Protestants was issued in 1681. The crown's response to the main wave came under James II, who authorised a nationwide church collection for the refugees.
findings.evidence: regnal dates of Charles II (d. 6 Feb 1685) against the revocation of the Edict of Nantes (Oct 1685)

findings.claim: Cattelena of Almondsbury, an independent Black woman in Bristol
findings.truth: Almondsbury is in Gloucestershire, just outside Bristol, not in the city.
findings.evidence: location of Almondsbury

findings.claim: Three 'Describe two features' questions on thematic content and two 'Explain why' questions set at 8 marks; several mark schemes credit Charles II with the post-1685 welcome
findings.truth: Rebuilt to the thematic forms, with the Charles II error removed from the mark schemes.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section; regnal dates of Charles II

findings.claim: anti-Italian rioting flared in Manchester in 1894; German bakers were attacked during periodic spy scares from the 1880s
findings.truth: Neither event can be traced. The German spy scare belongs to the 1900s and the attacks on German-owned shops to the anti-German riots of 1915, both outside this lesson's period. Replaced with the documented pattern: the public campaign against Italian street musicians in London, and press campaigns against 'pauper aliens' from the 1880s.
findings.evidence: no source found for either event; anti-German riots in Britain date from 1915

findings.claim: the Ayahs' Home in Hackney was set up to support stranded women
findings.truth: The London City Mission's Ayahs' Home stood at Aldgate through the nineteenth century and moved to Hackney only in 1900, after this lesson's period. Changed to 'east London'.
findings.evidence: history of the Ayahs' Home, London City Mission

findings.claim: Manchester's population grew from around 25,000 in 1772 to nearly 250,000 by 1851
findings.truth: The 1851 borough figure was over 300,000. The 1772 figure is right and the point about explosive growth stands, so the figure is flagged rather than changed.
findings.evidence: 1851 census, Manchester borough

findings.claim: Three 'Describe two features' questions on thematic content, two 'Explain why' questions at 8 marks, and two mark schemes repeating the untraceable 1894 Manchester riot
findings.truth: Rebuilt to the thematic forms with the invented event removed.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section

findings.claim: During the worst Famine years, 1846-47, perhaps 300,000 Irish migrants landed in Liverpool ... The Liverpool Select Vestry recorded over 300,000 Irish receiving poor relief in 1846 alone
findings.truth: Almost 300,000 Irish migrants landed at Liverpool in 1847, the worst single year. The relief figure repeats the arrival figure and dates it a year early; no source gives 300,000 relieved in 1846, so the number has been removed rather than replaced.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'History of Liverpool' ('Almost 300,000 arrived in 1847')

findings.claim: the city sent two Irish Nationalist MPs to Westminster between 1885 and 1929
findings.truth: One seat, Liverpool Scotland, returned one Irish Nationalist MP: T. P. O'Connor held it from 1885 until his death in 1929. It was the only Irish Nationalist seat in Britain outside Ireland.
findings.evidence: T. P. O'Connor's tenure of the Liverpool Scotland seat, 1885-1929

findings.claim: Three 'Describe two features' questions on thematic content and two 'Explain why' questions set at 8 marks; four mark schemes repeat the misdated relief figure or the plural MPs
findings.truth: Rebuilt to the thematic forms with both errors corrected.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section

findings.claim: In 1902 the British Brothers' League was founded by Major William Evans-Gordon, the Conservative MP for Stepney
findings.truth: The League was founded in the East End in May 1901 by William Stanley Shaw. Evans-Gordon, MP for Stepney, was its leading champion in Parliament, not its founder. The lesson's own glossary, conclusion and knowledge check already say 1901, so the content also contradicted itself.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, "British Brothers' League"

findings.claim: 'Yiddish press' defined as 'Jewish newspaper published in London from 1889'
findings.truth: The term names a whole press, not one paper, and the date is wrong for the Yidisher Ekspres, which moved to London in 1899. Redefined as the Yiddish-language papers of the East End.
findings.evidence: publication history of Der Yidisher Ekspres

findings.claim: Three 'Describe two features' questions on thematic content and two 'Explain why' questions set at 8 marks; one mark scheme names Evans-Gordon as founder
findings.truth: Rebuilt to the thematic forms with the founder corrected.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section

findings.claim: the Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury with 492 mainly Jamaican passengers
findings.truth: The ship's landing cards record 1,027 passengers (plus two stowaways) disembarking on 22 June 1948, of whom 802 gave a Caribbean country as their last place of residence. The figure of 492 comes from 1948 newspaper reports, which variously said 'more than 400', '430' or '500'.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'HMT Empire Windrush', citing the ship's manifest held at the National Archives

findings.claim: the 2021 EU Settlement Scheme brought an end to free movement
findings.truth: Free movement ended on 31 December 2020. The EU Settlement Scheme opened in 2019 and closed to most applicants on 30 June 2021; it recorded people's status rather than ending free movement.
findings.evidence: UK exit from the EU single market, 31 December 2020

findings.claim: Three 'Describe two features' questions on thematic content and two 'Explain why' questions set at 8 marks; mark schemes repeat the 492 figure
findings.truth: Rebuilt to the thematic forms with the passenger figure corrected.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section

findings.claim: Paul Stephenson ... later the first Black recipient of the OBE for services to the equal-opportunities movement
findings.truth: Stephenson received an OBE in the 2009 New Year Honours for services to equal opportunities and community relations in Bristol. He was not the first Black recipient of the honour, and no source supports that claim.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Bristol Bus Boycott'

findings.claim: Guy Bailey ... was openly turned away on 30 April 1963 because of his race. Stephenson then announced a public boycott
findings.truth: 30 April 1963 is the day the boycott began. Stephenson announced it at a press conference on 29 April, so the refused interview came before that date, not after it. The lesson had the trigger happening after the protest it triggered.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Bristol Bus Boycott' (announced 29 April, began 30 April, ended 28 August 1963)

findings.claim: an advertisement in the Ugandan newspaper Argus
findings.truth: The paper was the Uganda Argus.
findings.evidence: title of the Uganda Argus

findings.claim: Three 'Describe two features' questions on thematic content, an 'Explain the importance' question, and 'Explain why' set at 8 marks
findings.truth: 'Explain the importance' is not a form set on this paper. Rebuilt to the thematic forms with the OBE and Guy Bailey errors corrected.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section

findings.claim: For the 4-mark Inference question, lead with one inferred conclusion supported by a quoted detail
findings.truth: This paper sets no inference question. The historic environment section is worth 16 marks in three questions: 'Describe two features' (4), 'How useful are Sources A and B' (8) and 'How could you follow up Source B' (4).
findings.evidence: spec assessment section, Paper 1 Section A

findings.claim: One question typed '12 marks - Historic Environment Essay'; the source question offers a single source
findings.truth: The historic environment section sets no essay, and the 8-mark source question always gives two sources, A and B. Rebuilt to the three real forms, with a second composed source added and both labelled as composed.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section, Paper 1 Section A

findings.claim: police records (e.g. MEPO 2/9838)
findings.truth: The catalogue reference could not be verified. Metropolitan Police files on Notting Hill were released in 2002, so the general pointer stands but the invented-looking reference is removed.
findings.evidence: no confirmation of this reference in accessible catalogues; the 2002 release is documented

findings.claim: Powis Square, Powis Terrace and Colville Square - built in the 1850s
findings.truth: The Colville and Powis streets were built mainly in the 1860s. Softened to 'the mid-nineteenth century', which is safe for either dating.
findings.evidence: Colville conservation area building history

findings.claim: Restaurants such as El Rio on Westbourne Park Road and the Rio cafe on Notting Hill Gate became known across London - The Rio was used as a meeting place
findings.truth: One establishment has been split into two. Frank Crichlow ran the El Rio cafe on Westbourne Park Road; there was no separate 'Rio cafe on Notting Hill Gate'. The lesson's own later paragraph names only the El Rio.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction within the lesson: the All Saints Road section names only the El Rio on Westbourne Park Road

findings.claim: Ruth Glass's 1960 study Newcomers noted that the area's Caribbean economy was 'parallel rather than separate'
findings.truth: The quotation cannot be traced to Glass. Presented as a direct quotation it is a fabricated attribution, so the quotation marks have been removed and the point kept as a paraphrase.
findings.evidence: no traceable source for the phrase in Ruth Glass, Newcomers (1960)

findings.claim: the weekly pot was £24 (roughly the price of a second-hand car in 1960)
findings.truth: £24 in 1960 was well under two weeks' average earnings for a manual worker and nowhere near the price of a car. The comparison is replaced with a wage comparison.
findings.evidence: average weekly manual earnings in Britain in 1960 (about £14-15)

findings.claim: One question typed '12 marks - Historic Environment Essay' and one 'Explain why' at 8 marks in a historic environment lesson; the source question offers a single source
findings.truth: This section sets only the 4-mark 'Describe two features', the 8-mark two-source question and the 4-mark follow-up. Rebuilt to those forms.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section, Paper 1 Section A

findings.claim: nine white men were sentenced to four years each by Mr Justice Salmon
findings.truth: Each of the nine was sentenced to five years in prison and ordered to pay £500. The severity is the point of the example, so the wrong figure weakens it.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Notting Hill race riots': 'Each of the youths were sentenced to five years in prison and was ordered to pay £500.'

findings.claim: the police later acknowledged in the Met file MEPO 2/9838 that the violence was largely white-led rather than two-sided
findings.truth: The opposite is on record. Metropolitan Police files released in 2002 show senior officers assuring the Home Secretary, Rab Butler, that there was little or no racial motive behind the disturbances, despite the contrary evidence of individual officers. The catalogue reference could not be verified either.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Notting Hill race riots' (files released 2002)

findings.claim: Mosley received 2,821 votes - about 8% of the constituency total - finishing third ... He finished third, ahead of the Liberal candidate
findings.truth: Mosley finished fourth and last. The 1959 Kensington North result was Labour 14,925, Conservative 14,048, Liberal 3,118 and Union Movement (Mosley) 2,821. At 8.08% he fell below the one-eighth threshold and lost his deposit. The vote total and percentage in the lesson are right; the placing is not.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Kensington North (UK Parliament constituency)', 1959 result

findings.claim: Attacks ran across nine consecutive nights from 30 August to 5 September
findings.truth: 30 August to 5 September is seven nights, not nine, and the attacks began on 29 August. The internal arithmetic did not work.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Notting Hill race riots' (29 August to 5 September 1958)

findings.claim: The Met's policing ... was not yet on the legal record as institutionally racist - that judicial recognition would come in 1971
findings.truth: What the judge acknowledged in 1971 was evidence of racial hatred, not institutional racism. 'Institutional racism' entered official British use with the Macpherson report in 1999, so the sentence puts a later idea into a 1971 courtroom.
findings.evidence: Mangrove Nine trial, December 1971; Macpherson report, 1999

findings.claim: Two 'Explain why' questions at 8 marks, a '12 marks - Historic Environment Essay' and a 16-mark judgement question in a historic environment lesson; one mark scheme cites the British Brothers' League as a cause of tension in 1958-70
findings.truth: This section sets only the 4-mark 'Describe two features', the 8-mark two-source question and the 4-mark follow-up. The British Brothers' League was defunct after 1905; the anti-immigrant groups active in Notting Hill were Mosley's Union Movement and Colin Jordan's White Defence League.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section; the specification names Mosley's Union Movement for this site

findings.claim: Two were acquitted on all counts; the others received suspended sentences for lesser offences
findings.truth: Five of the nine were acquitted on all charges. Four - Rupert Boyce, Rhodan Gordon, Anthony Innis and Althea Jones-LeCointe - were convicted of lesser offences such as affray and assaulting police officers and received suspended sentences.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Mangrove Nine'

findings.claim: The Met had to apologise
findings.truth: There was no apology. The Metropolitan Police tried to have the judge's remark about racial hatred withdrawn and failed.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Mangrove Nine': 'The Metropolitan Police attempted to have this remark withdrawn but failed.'

findings.claim: The defence successfully demanded an all-Black jury (denied)
findings.truth: The demand was refused. The defendants then challenged 63 potential jurors over their understanding of 'black power', which left two Black jurors on the panel of twelve. The sentence as written contradicts itself.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Mangrove Nine'

findings.claim: the actress Diana Ross
findings.truth: Diana Ross is a singer, known first with the Supremes.
findings.evidence: Diana Ross's career

findings.claim: In October 1971 the Old Bailey jury acquitted the Mangrove Nine
findings.truth: The trial opened on 5 October 1971 and ran for 55 days; the verdict came in December 1971. The lesson's own content gives the 55-day length, so the knowledge check contradicted it.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Mangrove Nine' (trial opened 5 October 1971, lasted 55 days)

findings.claim: An 8-mark 'Explain why', a '12 marks - Historic Environment Essay' and a 16-mark judgement question in a historic environment lesson; the source question offers a single source; one mark scheme dates Martin Luther King's London visit to 1965
findings.truth: This section sets only the 4-mark 'Describe two features', the 8-mark two-source question and the 4-mark follow-up. King preached at St Paul's Cathedral in December 1964.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section; Martin Luther King's London visit, December 1964

summary: Fourteen lessons checked against the Edexcel 1HI0 specification and external sources. The dominant problem is exam form: 56 of the 84 practice questions were in forms this paper never sets - 'Describe two features' applied to the thematic study, 'Explain why' priced at 8 marks instead of 12, 'Explain the importance', a 12-mark historic environment essay and an inference question, both of which do not exist - and every one has been rebuilt to the real forms with a new mark scheme. Alongside that, 20 factual errors were corrected, the heaviest being the Windrush passenger figure, the Steelyard privileges attributed to a king who was already dead, Charles II welcoming refugees eight months after his own death, the Notting Hill sentences, Mosley's placing in 1959, the Mangrove Nine verdict split and a supposed Met apology that never happened. Two invented events, one invented quotation, one unverified archive reference and a claim about a police file that said the opposite of what was asserted were removed.
